summary: Instagram is doing most of the work: nearly every video gets 1,000+ views there, while YouTube Shorts mostly gets under 100 per video. The best videos use a surprising 'it doesn't X, it only Y' claim or a robot/clap-switch demo that people can picture instantly, and they get likes, saves and shares. Dry, generic 'How does X work?' titles about everyday places (lift, mall door, tap, smoke detector) get few views and almost no engagement, and the one English video did poorly on YouTube and wasn't posted on Instagram.
winningPattern: Hindi, Instagram-first. Hands-on maker subjects (robots, clap switch, mic, PIR/IR sensors) with a counter-intuitive hook like 'X doesn't do A, it only does B' or a funny personified line ('Line follower has no brain'). Short Hinglish titles with one emoji and a clear, concrete object. Videos with a visible behaviour (robot falling, clap/whistle triggering) earn the most likes, saves and shares.
doMore: Open with a 'doesn't see/hear/think, only does Y' contradiction in the first line
Pick robot and maker-project subjects where the audience can see something happen (falls, turns, triggers)
Make follow-ups to winners: gyro, clap switch and PIR each have more angles (balancing, filters, tuning)
End with a save-worthy takeaway such as a wiring tip or a 'try this at home' test to boost saves and shares
Cross-check why YouTube lags: test a stronger first-second visual and a shorter title on YT for the same winning topics
stopDoing: Generic 'Kaise kaam karta hai?' titles about public-place gadgets (lift, mall door, washroom tap)
Posting near-duplicate topics (two smoke alarm, two IR, two tap videos) within days of each other
Switching to English without a plan; keep Hindi until the audience proves otherwise
